Urfer SR.lab_name: Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Urfer SR.role: Veterinarian and epidemiologist of aging at the University of Washington who led the first placebo-controlled rapamycin trial in pet dogs, an early step of the Dog Aging Project
Urfer SR.sub: Acting Assistant Professor, Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, University of Washington (since 2022) · Senior Fellow, Department of Pathology, University of Washington (2016–2019) · postdoc, Department of Pathology, University of Washington (2008–2012) · postdoc, National Human Genome Research Institute, NIH (2007–2008) · Dr. med. vet., University of Bern (2007)
story: Rapamycin extends lifespan in mice, but mice live in cages and die young. Pet dogs share our homes, our air and often our food, and they age faster than we do, so they are a useful middle step between lab animals and people. In 2017 Silvan Urfer was first author of the trial that tested this idea for the first time (URF2017). Twenty-four healthy middle-aged companion dogs received either low-dose rapamycin or a placebo for 10 weeks, and neither owners nor vets knew which. The treated dogs showed no clinical side effects, and heart ultrasound (echocardiography) hinted at better heart function. With so few dogs and such a short course, the study shows that a larger trial is safe to attempt, not that rapamycin slows aging in dogs.

Urfer trained as a veterinarian at the University of Bern in Switzerland and earned the Dr. med. vet. doctorate there in 2007 with work in population genetics. After a short postdoc at the National Human Genome Research Institute in Bethesda, Urfer moved to the Department of Pathology at the University of Washington in Seattle, first as a postdoc and later as a senior fellow, working with Matt Kaeberlein's group on the dog studies that grew into the Dog Aging Project.

Since 2022 Urfer has been an Acting Assistant Professor in the Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology at the University of Washington. The faculty page lists lifespan and survival analysis, comparative medicine, epidemiology, rapamycin and canine cognitive dysfunction, the dog form of dementia, among the research interests.

highlights.URF2017: First author: ran the 10-week placebo-controlled rapamycin trial in 24 middle-aged pet dogs, which found no clinical side effects and possible gains in heart function.

Kim YC.lab_name: Vallon Lab, Division of Nephrology and Hypertension, University of California San Diego and VA San Diego Healthcare System (La Jolla, California, USA)
Kim YC.role: Cell biologist who studied mTOR and autophagy in Kun-Liang Guan's lab at UC San Diego and later moved to kidney research in Volker Vallon's group
Kim YC.sub: Division of Nephrology and Hypertension, UC San Diego, and VA San Diego Healthcare System (papers with Volker Vallon, 2024–2026) · Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, UC San Diego (Kun-Liang Guan lab, papers 2013–2015)
story: mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, only switches on when amino acids are around. Before 2015 the accepted route was the Rag GTPases, small switch proteins that bring mTORC1 to the surface of the lysosome. The Atlas study JEW2015 in Science, from Kun-Liang Guan's lab, showed that two amino acids use different routes. Leucine works through the Rags, but glutamine could still turn on mTORC1 in cells that lacked Rags, through a pathway that needed another small GTPase, Arf1. Young Chul Kim was second author. The work was done in cultured cells.

In the Guan lab Kim also wrote, with Guan, a 2015 review on mTOR as a drug target for controlling autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and co-authored studies on how the energy sensor AMPK steers different Vps34 complexes during starvation and on how Wnt signals switch on the growth regulators YAP and TAZ. The 2015 Cell paper already listed a second address at the Veterans Medical Research Foundation in San Diego.

Later PubMed records place Kim at the Division of Nephrology and Hypertension of UC San Diego and the VA San Diego Healthcare System, in Volker Vallon's group. That work studies the kidney: how diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitor drugs and GLP1 receptor drugs change gene activity in the proximal tubule, and how glucagon-receptor agonists affect kidney injury in mice.

highlights.JEW2015: Second author: helped show in cultured cells that glutamine can activate mTORC1 without the Rag GTPases, through Arf1, unlike leucine.

Kim YC.note: Identity link between the Guan-lab Young Chul Kim and the Vallon-lab (VA San Diego nephrology) Young Chul Kim rests on: one UCSD Profiles page listing both Guan as co-author and kidney topics, and the 2015 Cell paper giving a VA-linked San Diego address. No official bio page found. Please confirm before publishing the kidney part.

Park HW.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry, College of Life Science and Biotechnology, Yonsei University (Seoul, South Korea)
Park HW.role: Biochemist at Yonsei University who trained with Kun-Liang Guan on the Hippo-YAP/TAZ growth pathway and now studies how cancer cells change their signalling and metabolism to spread
Park HW.sub: Department of Biochemistry, College of Life Science and Biotechnology, Yonsei University, Seoul (papers since 2020) · postdoc, Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, UC San Diego (Kun-Liang Guan lab, papers to 2015)
story: The Atlas study JEW2015 in Science, from Kun-Liang Guan's lab at UC San Diego, asked how different amino acids switch on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex. Leucine acted through the Rag GTPases, the usual route to the lysosome, while glutamine could activate mTORC1 in cells without Rags, through a route that needed the small GTPase Arf1. Hyun Woo Park was a co-author. The experiments were done in cultured cells.

Park's main work in the Guan lab was on the Hippo pathway and its targets YAP and TAZ, proteins that control organ size and are often overactive in cancer. As first author of a 2015 Cell paper, Park showed that the alternative Wnt signals Wnt5a/b and Wnt3a switch on YAP/TAZ through a chain of receptors, G proteins and Rho GTPases, separate from the classic beta-catenin route.

Park now runs a group in the Department of Biochemistry at Yonsei University in Seoul. Recent papers from the group, some still with Guan as co-author, describe an adherent-to-suspension transition in which solid tumour cells borrow blood-cell gene programs, switch off YAP/TEAD-driven adhesion genes and detach to become circulating tumour cells. The group has also reviewed how signalling pathways such as PI3K/AKT and Hippo rewire cancer metabolism.

highlights.JEW2015: Co-author: part of the Guan-lab team that showed in cultured cells that glutamine activates mTORC1 through Arf1 without the Rag GTPases.

Elshal M.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (Mansoura, Egypt)
Elshal M.role: Pharmacologist at Mansoura University who tests whether existing drugs can protect the brain, liver and other organs in rodent models of disease
Elshal M.sub: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (papers 2024–2026)
story: Epilepsy often develops over time after an injury or a series of seizures, a process called epileptogenesis. In the Atlas study MADKOUR2026, Mahmoud Elshal was last author, the position that usually marks the senior scientist who supervised the work. Rats received repeated small doses of PTZ, a chemical that lowers the seizure threshold, so that seizures grow stronger with each dose (kindling). Rats pre-treated with carvedilol, a common heart and blood-pressure drug, had lower seizure scores, less damage in the hippocampus, the memory region of the brain, and less inflammation driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome. Levels of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway proteins changed at the same time. The authors state that these are associations and do not prove that mTOR signalling causes the benefit.

Elshal works in the Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology of the Faculty of Pharmacy at Mansoura University in Egypt. PubMed lists dozens of papers with this affiliation, most of them rodent studies that repurpose approved drugs. In 2026 the same team reported that empagliflozin, a diabetes drug, reduced PTZ-induced seizures in rats and strengthened the effect of the antiseizure drug levetiracetam, and a 2024 study in mice found that the diabetes drug sitagliptin protected the liver against chemically induced cholestasis, a blockage of bile flow. No official profile page was found.

highlights.MADKOUR2026: Last author: supervised the rat study in which carvedilol lowered PTZ-kindled seizures, hippocampal damage and NLRP3 inflammation, alongside changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related proteins.

sources: PubMed search Elshal M[Author] AND Mansoura[Affiliation] (47 records)

Madkour AH.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (Mansoura, Egypt)
Madkour AH.role: Pharmacologist at Mansoura University who tests approved drugs as protection against seizures and kidney injury in rats
Madkour AH.sub: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (papers 2022–2026) · Faculty of Health Science Technology, Mansoura National University (2026)
story: Ahmed Madkour was first author of the Atlas study MADKOUR2026 in Scientific Reports, which asked whether carvedilol, a beta-blocker used for heart failure and high blood pressure, could slow the development of epilepsy. Rats received repeated doses of PTZ, a chemical that makes seizures easier to trigger, until seizures became stronger over time (kindling). Rats given carvedilol beforehand had lower seizure scores, less damage in the hippocampus and less inflammation linked to the NLRP3 inflammasome, an alarm system of immune cells. Proteins of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, which controls cell growth and survival, changed at the same time. The authors say the study shows associations only, so it does not prove that mTOR signalling is the reason carvedilol helped.

PubMed lists Madkour at the Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology of the Faculty of Pharmacy at Mansoura University, Egypt, from 2022 onward. An earlier first-author paper (2022) found that lactoferrin, an iron-binding milk protein, protected rat kidneys in a dose-dependent way after muscle breakdown caused by glycerol. A 2026 first-author paper in Neurotoxicology, again with Mahmoud Elshal, reported that the diabetes drug empagliflozin reduced PTZ-induced seizures in rats and worked best together with a lower dose of levetiracetam. That paper also lists the Faculty of Health Science Technology at Mansoura National University. No official profile page was found.

highlights.MADKOUR2026: First author: ran the rat PTZ-kindling study in which carvedilol lowered seizure scores, hippocampal damage and NLRP3 inflammation, with matching changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related proteins.

Cui X.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology, College of Pharmacy, Beihua University (Jilin, China)
Cui X.role: Pharmacologist at Beihua University who studies how plant-derived compounds protect the kidney and heart from damage caused by high blood pressure in mice
Cui X.sub: Department of Pharmacology, College of Pharmacy, Beihua University, Jilin (papers 2026)
story: High blood pressure slowly damages the kidney. In the Atlas study CUI2026 in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology, Xiaoli Cui was first author. Mice received angiotensin II, a hormone that raises blood pressure and injures the kidney. Treatment with forsythoside A, a compound from the medicinal plant Forsythia, protected the kidney. The team reports that forsythoside A binds a protein called ASCL1 and so blocks a downstream CCNB1/mTOR axis. With mTOR held back, the cells cleared more damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) and suffered less ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Blood pressure itself did not fall, so the protection came from inside the kidney cells. The work was done in mice and cells.

Cui works in the Department of Pharmacology of the College of Pharmacy at Beihua University in Jilin, China, with Mengyang Wang, the senior author of CUI2026. In 2026 the same group reported that fangchinoline, an alkaloid from the plant Stephania tetrandra, protected mouse hearts from angiotensin II-induced heart failure through mitophagy and less ferroptosis, and that schisandrin B eased fatty liver disease in mice through the receptor PPAR-gamma. No official profile page was found, so the career path before 2026 is not known.

highlights.CUI2026: First author: led the mouse study in which forsythoside A blocked an ASCL1-CCNB1/mTOR axis, increased mitophagy and reduced ferroptosis in kidneys damaged by angiotensin II.

Gan X.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Gan X.role: Biochemist at Fudan University who showed as a Yale postdoc that the lipid messenger PIP3 directly switches on mTORC2, and who now studies Wnt and mTORC2 signalling in metabolism
Gan X.sub: Researcher, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Fudan University (since 2013) · postdoc, Yale University School of Medicine (2009–2013) · PhD in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences (2008)
story: mTORC2 is the second mTOR complex. One of its main jobs is to switch on Akt, a kinase that tells cells to take up sugar, grow and survive. By 2011 it was known that growth factors acting through PI3K turn on mTORC2, but not how. PI3K makes a lipid called PIP3 in the cell membrane. In the Atlas study GAN2011, Xiaoqing Gan, working in Dianqing Wu's lab at Yale, showed in cultured cells and in test-tube kinase assays that PIP3 directly raises the activity of mTORC2. This gave a simple chemical link between PI3K and mTORC2.

Gan earned a PhD in biochemistry and molecular biology at the Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2008 and was a postdoc at Yale University School of Medicine from 2009 to 2013.

Since 2013 Gan has been a researcher (principal investigator) in the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology of the School of Basic Medical Sciences at Fudan University in Shanghai. The group works on metabolism and cell signalling, with themes that include Wnt signalling in stem cell differentiation, communication between bone and brown fat, and G protein-coupled receptor and mTORC2 signalling.

highlights.GAN2011: First author: showed in cells and in kinase assays that the lipid PIP3 directly stimulates mTORC2, linking PI3K to mTORC2.

Gan X.note: Fudan page does not name the Yale supervisor; Dianqing Wu is inferred from the last author of GAN2011 (same years, same place).

Drummond MJ.lab_name: Drummond Lab, Department of Physical Therapy and Athletic Training, University of Utah (Salt Lake City, Utah, USA)
Drummond MJ.role: Muscle physiologist at the University of Utah who studies why older muscle wastes during inactivity and recovers poorly, and who showed that mTORC1 drives part of the protein-building response to exercise in humans
Drummond MJ.sub: Professor, Department of Physical Therapy and Athletic Training, University of Utah · postdoc in muscle biology, University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston (to 2008) · PhD in Exercise Sciences, Brigham Young University (2006)
story: When you lift weights, your muscles start building new protein within an hour or two. In 2009, Micah Drummond, then at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston with Blake Rasmussen, tested whether mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is needed for that response in people (DRU2009). Healthy volunteers took a single dose of rapamycin before a session of resistance exercise. In the control group, muscle protein synthesis rose by about 40% in the first one to two hours. Rapamycin blocked that rise. Rapamycin also blunted ERK1/2 and MNK1 signalling, so the authors concluded that mTORC1 drives the response only in part. The study measured protein synthesis over a few hours, not muscle growth over weeks.

Drummond studied at California Lutheran University, earned a PhD in exercise sciences at Brigham Young University in 2006 and trained in muscle biology at the University of Texas Medical Branch until 2008.

At the University of Utah, Drummond is a Professor of Physical Therapy and Athletic Training, with adjunct appointments in nutrition and integrative physiology and other departments. The lab studies how aging, physical inactivity and immune changes combine to cause muscle loss and poor recovery after disuse, such as bed rest, hospital stays or surgery, with a focus on inflammation, cellular senescence and metabolic disease in aged rodents and in people.

highlights.DRU2009: First author: showed in healthy volunteers that rapamycin blocks the early rise in muscle protein synthesis after resistance exercise.

Drummond MJ.note: Utah faculty profile also lists a Professor of Pathology appointment dated 1 Oct 2026; shown title kept as Physical Therapy and Athletic Training per the bioscience page.

Hosokawa N.lab_name: Department of Physiology and Cell Biology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (Tokyo, Japan)
Hosokawa N.role: Cell biologist who, in Noboru Mizushima's lab, showed how mTORC1 directly holds the autophagy starter complex in check and helped discover the autophagy protein Atg101
Hosokawa N.sub: Department of Physiology and Cell Biology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (Noboru Mizushima lab, 2009, at the time of the study) · Department of Bioregulation and Metabolism, Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Medical Science (2007)
story: Autophagy is the cell's recycling system: it wraps worn-out parts in a membrane and breaks them down for raw materials. Cells should only do this when food is short, so something has to keep autophagy off when nutrients are plentiful. In 2009, Nao Hosokawa, first author of the Atlas study HOS2009 from Noboru Mizushima's lab, showed in cultured cells how mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, does it. The autophagy starter kinase ULK1 sits in a large complex with Atg13 and FIP200. When nutrients are present, mTORC1 physically joins this complex and adds phosphate groups to ULK1 and Atg13, which keeps them inactive. Starvation or the drug rapamycin releases this brake, and autophagy begins. This gave a direct molecular link between nutrient sensing and autophagy.

In the same year Hosokawa was also first author of a paper in Autophagy that identified Atg101, a new mammalian protein that binds Atg13 and is needed for autophagy to proceed. An earlier first-author paper from 2007, at the Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Medical Science and again with Mizushima, built mouse cell lines in which autophagy can be switched on and off with an antibiotic, and used them to show that autophagy helps cells shrink during starvation.
PubMed records under this name with autophagy work stop after 2009, and no later institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one at the time of the study.

highlights.HOS2009: First author: showed in cultured cells that mTORC1 binds the ULK1-Atg13-FIP200 complex when nutrients are plentiful and phosphorylates ULK1 and Atg13 to keep autophagy off.

Hosokawa N.note: Current position not found (web search budget ran out before a dedicated search; PubMed autophagy record ends in 2009).

Goberdhan DC.lab_name: Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health, University of Oxford (Oxford, England, United Kingdom)
Goberdhan DC.role: Oxford cell biologist who studies how amino acid transporters and the cell's secretory compartments control growth signalling, often using the fruit fly, and who argued that intracellular transporters mark where mTORC1 is switched on
Goberdhan DC.sub: Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health, University of Oxford (2025–2026) · Department of Physiology, Anatomy and Genetics, University of Oxford (papers to 2025)
story: mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is switched on by amino acids, but where in the cell does that happen? In a 2016 review in Cell Metabolism (GOB2016), written with Adrian Harris, Deborah Goberdhan argued that amino acid transporters sitting in the membranes of compartments inside the cell, such as late endosomes, lysosomes and the Golgi apparatus, mark the spots where mTORC1 is activated. The review proposed that different amino acids in different compartments may switch on different pools of mTORC1. It is a synthesis of existing evidence, not a new experiment.

Goberdhan has worked for many years in the Department of Physiology, Anatomy and Genetics at the University of Oxford, often with Clive Wilson, and has more than 50 papers in PubMed. The work moves between fly genetics and human cancer. With Harris, Goberdhan's group reported in 2020 that the glutamine transporter SNAT2 helps triple-negative breast cancer cells resist oxidative stress and is linked to worse survival. Goberdhan was also a co-author of MISEV2018, the international guidelines for research on extracellular vesicles, the small membrane packets that cells release.

More recent papers use the prostate-like secondary cells of male fruit flies to watch secretion live. A 2025 study in The EMBO Journal showed that the Alzheimer's protein APP and amyloid-beta disturb how dense-core secretory granules form in recycling endosomes, and a 2026 review proposed that faulty regulated secretion might start Alzheimer's pathology. These papers list Goberdhan at the Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health at Oxford.

highlights.GOB2016: First author: proposed in a review that amino acid transporters inside the cell mark the sites where mTORC1 is activated.

Caccamo A.lab_name: Department of Chemical, Biological, Pharmaceutical and Environmental Sciences, University of Messina (Messina, Italy)
Caccamo A.role: Neuroscientist who, with Salvatore Oddo, showed in Alzheimer's model mice that amyloid-beta and mTOR feed each other in a loop that rapamycin can break
Caccamo A.sub: Department of Chemical, Biological, Pharmaceutical and Environmental Sciences, University of Messina (papers 2024–2026) · ASU-Banner Neurodegenerative Disease Research Center, Arizona State University (papers to about 2020) · Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (2010)
story: Alzheimer's disease has two hallmarks: clumps of amyloid-beta outside nerve cells and tangles of the protein tau inside them. In a 2010 mouse study (CAC2010), Antonella Caccamo, first author in Salvatore Oddo's group at the University of Texas Health Science Center in San Antonio, found that the two are tied to mTOR in a loop. Amyloid-beta raised mTOR activity. High mTOR in turn blocked autophagy, the cell's clean-up process, so more amyloid and tau built up. In 3xTg-AD mice, a model that develops both hallmarks, rapamycin broke the loop, improved memory and lowered both amyloid-beta and tau. When autophagy was blocked, the drop in amyloid disappeared, which showed that autophagy was needed for the benefit. All of this was in mice, not in people.

Caccamo and Oddo later moved to the ASU-Banner Neurodegenerative Disease Research Center at Arizona State University, where they continued to publish together, including work on autophagy in Alzheimer's model mice.

PubMed records since 2024 list Caccamo, again with Oddo, at the Department of Chemical, Biological, Pharmaceutical and Environmental Sciences of the University of Messina in Italy. Recent work includes a 2024 review on DNA methylation and histone changes in Alzheimer's disease and a 2026 mouse study on the lipid enzyme diacylglycerol kinase theta, whose levels rose with amyloid and with activation of support cells called astrocytes in older APP/PS1 mice.

highlights.CAC2010: First author: showed in 3xTg-AD mice that amyloid-beta raises mTOR, that high mTOR blocks autophagy, and that rapamycin breaks this loop and improves memory.

sources: PubMed: Caccamo A[Author] AND Oddo S[Author] AND Arizona[Affiliation] (13 records)
Caccamo A.note: CAC2010 (PMID 20178983) is not flagged as retracted in PubMed. Other, non-Atlas Caccamo/Oddo papers are retracted (e.g. PMID 29729422, retraction note PMID 32782379; PubMed also lists 27573878, 16331665, 15139853 under retraction/concern types). Curator may want to double-check the 2012 Caccamo Atlas record.

Spilman P.lab_name: Drug Discovery Lab, Department of Neurology, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Spilman P.role: Neuroscientist who showed, with Veronica Galvan, that long-term rapamycin prevents memory loss in an Alzheimer's mouse model, and who later worked with Dale Bredesen on Alzheimer's drug discovery
Spilman P.sub: Drug Discovery Lab, Department of Neurology, UCLA (2025) · Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (2010)
story: By 2010 rapamycin was known to extend lifespan in mice, but did it help with a specific disease of old age? In the Atlas study SPI2010, Patricia Spilman was first author and Veronica Galvan senior author. Mice engineered to model Alzheimer's disease were fed rapamycin for a long time. The treated mice did not develop the memory problems seen in untreated animals, and they had less amyloid-beta, the protein that forms plaques in the Alzheimer's brain. Neurons of treated mice showed more autophagy, the cell's clean-up process, which suggests one way the drug helped. The study was done in mice and does not show the same effect in people.

PubMed lists 14 papers that Spilman co-authored with Galvan or with Dale Bredesen, from 2007 to 2025. In 2025 Spilman was a co-author of a Scientific Reports paper from the Drug Discovery Lab in UCLA's Department of Neurology describing DDL-218, an orally active small molecule that raised levels of the protein SirT1 in nerve cells carrying ApoE4, the main genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, and in a mouse model.
No official profile page was found, so the current position is not confirmed.

highlights.SPI2010: First author: showed that long-term rapamycin prevented memory deficits and lowered amyloid-beta in an Alzheimer's mouse model, with more autophagy in neurons.

sources: PubMed: Spilman P[Author] AND (Bredesen DE[Author] OR Galvan V[Author]) (14 records)
Spilman P.note: A Patricia Spilman at ImmunityBio (Culver City) appears on 2026 urology/immunotherapy papers (e.g. PMID 42635166). Likely the same person but no second tie found, so not used.

Gao X.lab_name: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas, Texas, USA)
Gao X.role: Geneticist who, in Duojia Pan's lab, used fruit flies and mammalian cells to show that the tumour suppressors Tsc1 and Tsc2 restrain TOR signalling and make it sensitive to amino acids
Gao X.sub: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center at Dallas (Duojia Pan lab, papers 2000–2005, at the time of the study)
story: Tuberous sclerosis complex is an inherited disease in which benign tumours grow in the brain, skin, kidneys and other organs. It is caused by faults in either of two genes, TSC1 or TSC2. Around 2002 the big question was how these two tumour suppressors hold back growth. In the Atlas study GAO2002 in Nature Cell Biology, Xinsheng Gao, first author in Duojia Pan's lab at UT Southwestern in Dallas, showed in fruit flies and mammalian cells that Tsc1 and Tsc2 can physically associate with TOR, the nutrient-sensing kinase, and act upstream of it in fly genetic tests. Cells lacking Tsc1 or Tsc2 had more activity of S6K, a kinase that TOR switches on, and this rise depended on TOR. Normally S6K switches off when cells are starved of amino acids, but cells without Tsc1 or Tsc2 kept it on. The work placed the TSC proteins in the nutrient-sensing TOR pathway, which later helped make rapamycin-type drugs a treatment option for tuberous sclerosis.

PubMed lists seven papers from 2000 to 2005 in which Gao and Pan appear together on fly growth control and the Tsc genes. No later record could be tied to this person with confidence, because the name is common, so the affiliation shown is the one at the time of the study.

highlights.GAO2002: First author: showed in flies and mammalian cells that Tsc1 and Tsc2 act upstream of TOR and that cells lacking them keep S6K active even without amino acids.

sources: PubMed: Gao X[Author] AND Pan D[Author] AND (Drosophila OR Tsc1 OR Tsc2), to 2008 (7 records)
Gao X.note: Current position unknown. The sentence about rapamycin-type drugs becoming a TSC treatment is general background, not from this paper; drop it if the curator prefers.

Chen K.lab_name: Department of Plastic Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (Wenzhou, China)
Chen K.role: Researcher in plastic surgery at Wenzhou Medical University and first author of a mouse study on engineered stem-cell exosomes that speed wound healing by changing fibroblast metabolism
Chen K.sub: Department of Plastic Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Chronic wounds, such as foot ulcers in people with diabetes, can stay open for months. In the Atlas study CHEN2026 in Cellular Signalling, Kewei Chen was first author. The team engineered adipose-derived stem cells, stem cells taken from fat tissue, so that the tiny vesicles they release (exosomes) carried FGF21, a hormone that affects energy use. When these exosomes were given to skin fibroblasts, the cells that rebuild tissue, the fibroblasts switched up glycolysis, the quick sugar-burning pathway, with the energy sensor AMPK turned on and mTOR signalling turned down. The fibroblasts divided and moved faster, and wounds in a mouse model closed sooner. The evidence comes from cells and mice.

PubMed lists Chen in the Department of Plastic Surgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University, with Li L as senior author. Because the name is very common, no other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, and no official profile page was found.

highlights.CHEN2026: First author: showed in fibroblasts and a mouse wound model that FGF21-loaded stem-cell exosomes boost glycolysis, activate AMPK, lower mTOR signalling and speed wound closure.

Javors MA.lab_name: Department of Psychiatry, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Javors MA.role: Pharmacologist at UT Health San Antonio whose laboratory measures drug levels in blood and tissue, including rapamycin in mouse lifespan studies and in the first rapamycin safety trial in older people
Javors MA.sub: Department of Psychiatry, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (papers 2015–2022)
story: A drug can only be judged if you know how much of it actually reaches the blood. Martin Javors appears as a co-author on rapamycin studies from San Antonio, where the measurement of drug levels is part of the work. In the Atlas pilot trial KRA2018, 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95 took daily rapamycin or placebo for at least eight weeks. The drug was well tolerated, with only small changes in red blood cells and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance over that short period. The trial was small and short and only checked safety, but it laid groundwork for larger human studies.

Javors is also a co-author of the Atlas study STR2022 from the NIA Interventions Testing Program, which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Rapamycin plus acarbose, a drug that slows sugar uptake from the gut, started at nine months of age gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone had given in earlier groups. In females the combination did about as well as rapamycin alone.

PubMed lists 16 papers with Javors that involve rapamycin, including earlier Interventions Testing Program reports such as the 2016 study in which metformin plus rapamycin extended mouse lifespan, and a 2015 study in which rapamycin shortened life in db/db mice, a model of type 2 diabetes. Most give the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio as the address. No official profile page was found.

highlights.KRA2018: Co-author: part of the team behind the pilot trial showing that eight weeks of daily rapamycin was well tolerated in healthy adults aged 70 to 95.
highlights.STR2022: Co-author: part of the Interventions Testing Program study in which rapamycin plus acarbose gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts.

sources: PubMed: Javors MA[Author] AND (rapamycin OR sirolimus) (16 records)
Javors MA.note: The statement that Javors' lab measures drug levels is inferred from his role pattern on these papers, not from an official page (web search budget ran out). Please verify or soften.

Fan W.lab_name: Laiho Lab, Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Fan W.role: Cancer biologist in Marikki Laiho's lab at Johns Hopkins who studies ribosome production as a weak point of cancer cells, and who showed how mTOR inhibition helps cells survive when ribosomes run short
Fan W.sub: Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Marikki Laiho lab, papers 2022–2026)
story: Ribosomes are the machines that build every protein in the cell, and cancer cells need huge numbers of them. Drugs that block ribosome production are being tested against cancer. In the Atlas study FAN2026 in Genes & Development, Wenjun Fan, first author in Marikki Laiho's lab, asked what happens to mTOR signalling when ribosome production fails. Turning mTORC1 off did not restore ribosome production. Instead it shifted the few ribosomes left away from 5'TOP mRNAs, a family of messages that normally take up a large share of ribosomes, and toward messages the cell needs to survive. The authors call this translational fitness. The work was done in cancer cells.

All of Fan's papers with Laiho in PubMed come from the Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences at Johns Hopkins. As first author in 2022, Fan used whole-genome data from 2,504 people in the 1000 Genomes Project to show that human ribosomal RNA genes vary much more between people than expected. A 2025 first-author paper in Cell Chemical Biology found that cancer cells with faulty RPL22, a ribosomal protein, are especially sensitive to drugs that block RNA polymerase I, the enzyme that makes ribosomal RNA, and that RPL22 also controls how many other messages are spliced. The Atlas paper also lists the University of Maryland School of Medicine.

highlights.FAN2026: First author: showed in cancer cells that mTORC1 inhibition redirects scarce ribosomes from 5'TOP mRNAs to survival transcripts when ribosome production fails.

sources: PubMed: Fan W[Author] AND Laiho M[Author] (6 records)

Huang C.lab_name: Department of Radiation Oncology, The Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University (Hohhot, China)
Huang C.role: Radiation oncology researcher in Hohhot and first author of a study linking the PIK3CA E545K mutation to faster growth and invasion of cervical cancer through AKT/mTOR signalling
Huang C.sub: Department of Radiation Oncology, The Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: PIK3CA is the gene for the catalytic part of PI3K, an enzyme at the top of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth pathway. Certain spelling mistakes in this gene, called hotspot mutations, keep the enzyme switched on. In the Atlas study HUANG2026 in Molecular Genetics and Genomics, Congxiu Huang was first author. The team sequenced tumours from 61 patients with cervical cancer and found PIK3CA among the most often mutated genes. They then put the E545K mutation, one of the common hotspots, into cervical cancer cell lines. The cells grew and invaded faster, died less, and showed stronger AKT/mTOR signalling. Human cancer cells grown as tumours in mice (a xenograft model) behaved the same way. The work suggests that patients whose tumours carry this mutation might be candidates for drugs against the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, but it did not test such drugs in patients.

PubMed lists Huang at the Department of Radiation Oncology of the Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University in Hohhot, with Sun X as senior author. Because the name is common, no other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, and no official profile page was found.

highlights.HUANG2026: First author: found PIK3CA among the most often mutated genes in 61 cervical tumours and showed in cells and xenografts that E545K drives growth and invasion through AKT/mTOR.

Aware C.lab_name: Lin Lab, Department of Radiology and NextGen Precision Health, University of Missouri (Columbia, Missouri, USA)
Aware C.role: Researcher in Ai-Ling Lin's group at the University of Missouri who studies how rapamycin and the gut microbiome affect brain blood flow and metabolism in people and mice at genetic risk of Alzheimer's disease
Aware C.sub: Department of Radiology and NextGen Precision Health, University of Missouri (Ai-Ling Lin lab, papers 2024–2026)
story: APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Carriers often show lower blood flow and weaker energy use in the brain years before any memory problems. In the Atlas study AWARE2026, Chetan Aware was first author of a small pilot trial at the University of Missouri. Twenty-three cognitively normal adults aged 45 to 65 took 1 mg of rapamycin a day for four weeks. In the nine APOE4 carriers, blood flow in several brain regions rose by more than 15%, while non-carriers showed no clear change. Blood markers of metabolism and inflammation improved, and the gut microbiome shifted. There was no placebo group and very few participants, so this is early evidence that needs a controlled trial.

Aware works in Ai-Ling Lin's group in the Department of Radiology and NextGen Precision Health at the University of Missouri. The group had earlier shown in mice carrying human APOE4 that 16 weeks of rapamycin improved mitochondrial function and nerve-cell signalling in the brain, with different effects in APOE3 mice; Aware was a co-author of that 2024 study. In 2026 Aware was first author of a mouse study in which gut bacteria taken from stroke patients sped up tau changes and brain inflammation in Alzheimer's model mice, pointing to the gut-brain connection as a possible link between stroke and later dementia. No official profile page was found.

highlights.AWARE2026: First author: ran the pilot trial in which four weeks of low-dose rapamycin raised brain blood flow in APOE4 carriers aged 45 to 65.

Aware C.note: A Chetan B. Aware at Shivaji University, Kolhapur, India appears on 2017-2019 biotechnology papers (e.g. PMID 29216550). Possibly the same person's earlier training, but no second tie found, so not used.

Ma XM.lab_name: Department of Research Oncology Diagnostics, Genentech (South San Francisco, California, USA)
Ma XM.role: Cell biologist who trained with John Blenis on how mTOR and S6K1 control protein synthesis, wrote a widely used review of mTOR-driven translation, and later worked in cancer research at Genentech
Ma XM.sub: Department of Research Oncology Diagnostics, Genentech (2009–2015) · John Blenis lab (papers 2008–2011)
story: Making protein is one of the most energy-hungry things a cell does, so cells only do it at full speed when conditions are good. mTOR is the sensor that decides. In 2009 Xiaoju Max Ma wrote, with John Blenis, a review in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology (MAX2009) that explains how mTOR takes in signals about nutrients, energy, stress and growth factors and passes them on to the protein-making machinery. It covers the two best-known mTORC1 targets, S6K1 and the 4E-BP proteins that hold back the start of translation. As a review, it summarises earlier experiments rather than reporting new ones.

PubMed lists four papers under this name tied to Blenis or Genentech: a 2008 research paper and the 2009 review with Blenis, the 2011 phosphoproteomics study that identified Grb10 as an mTORC1 target (also in the Atlas), and a 2015 Science Translational Medicine paper from Genentech and AbbVie on BCL-2 family inhibitors, cancer drugs that make tumour cells more likely to die. The 2009 review gives the Department of Research Oncology Diagnostics at Genentech as the address.
No current institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MAX2009: First author: wrote, with John Blenis, the review explaining how mTOR links nutrient, energy and growth signals to the control of protein synthesis.

sources: PubMed: Ma XM[Author] AND (Blenis J[Author] OR Genentech[Affiliation]) (4 records: 18423201, 19339977, 21659605, 25787766)
Ma XM.note: YUX2011 (PMID 21659605) also lists Ma XM; curator may want to add it to the profile timeline.

Gnant M.lab_name: Comprehensive Cancer Center, Medical University of Vienna (Vienna, Austria)
Gnant M.role: Breast cancer surgeon and trialist at the Medical University of Vienna, working with the Austrian Breast and Colorectal Cancer Study Group, and a co-author of BOLERO-2, the trial that brought the mTOR inhibitor everolimus into breast cancer treatment
Gnant M.sub: Comprehensive Cancer Center, Medical University of Vienna · Austrian Breast and Colorectal Cancer Study Group, Vienna · Department of Surgery, Medical University of Vienna (2014)
story: Most breast cancers grow in response to the hormone estrogen, and hormone therapy is the main treatment. Over time many tumours stop responding, and part of that resistance runs through mTOR. BOLERO-2 (BAS2012) was a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 postmenopausal women whose hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer had progressed on an aromatase inhibitor. Adding the mTOR inhibitor everolimus to the hormone drug exemestane more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again, 10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review. The result led to approval of the combination. Mouth sores (stomatitis) were the main side effect. Michael Gnant was one of the co-authors.

The final overall-survival report (PIC2014) found a median of 31.0 months with everolimus plus exemestane and 26.6 months with placebo plus exemestane. That gap was not statistically significant, so the drug delayed progression but was not shown to lengthen life. Both papers are human trials.

Gnant is based at the Comprehensive Cancer Center of the Medical University of Vienna and at the Austrian Breast and Colorectal Cancer Study Group (ABCSG), the national trials group; the 2014 report gave the Department of Surgery as the address. PubMed lists close to 100 papers with Gnant, Vienna and ABCSG, many of them large breast cancer trials and treatment guidelines, such as a 2026 Austrian consensus on CDK4/6 inhibitors after surgery for early breast cancer.

highlights.BAS2012: Co-author: part of the BOLERO-2 team showing that everolimus plus exemestane more than doubled progression-free survival in advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer.
highlights.PIC2014: Co-author: part of the team reporting that BOLERO-2's overall-survival gain (31.0 versus 26.6 months) was not statistically significant.

sources: PubMed: Gnant M[Author] AND Vienna[Affiliation] AND ABCSG (95 records)
Gnant M.note: Gnant's exact current title and ABCSG role were not confirmed on an official page (web search budget ran out); text says 'working with' the ABCSG.

Wang Q.lab_name: Yang Lab, Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology, College of Medicine, University of Kentucky (Lexington, Kentucky, USA)
Wang Q.role: Cancer biologist in Hsin-Sheng Yang's lab at the University of Kentucky who studies how the tumour suppressor Pdcd4 holds back mTORC2 signalling, protein synthesis and cancer cell invasion
Wang Q.sub: Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology and Markey Cancer Center, College of Medicine, University of Kentucky (Hsin-Sheng Yang lab, papers 2017–2026)
story: Cancer cells burn sugar fast, even when oxygen is plentiful, a habit called aerobic glycolysis. In the Atlas study WANG2026B in Neoplasia, Qing Wang was first author in Hsin-Sheng Yang's lab. The team showed in non-small cell lung cancer cells and in tumours grown in mice that the tumour suppressor Pdcd4 binds Rictor, the core partner of mTOR in the mTORC2 complex, through three positively charged amino acids (R105, K108 and R110). This binding breaks up mTORC2 and lowers its activity. Less mTORC2 means less PFKFB3, an enzyme that speeds up glycolysis, so the cancer cells use less sugar and grow more slowly. The work was done in cells and mouse xenografts.

Wang has worked with Yang in the Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology at the University of Kentucky for several years; PubMed lists 18 papers with both names and this address. Much of the work is on Pdcd4 in colorectal cancer. A 2025 first-author paper showed that Pdcd4 blocks translation of Slug, a protein that helps cancer cells invade, through the 5' untranslated region of its messenger RNA. A 2020 first-author paper found that blocking the IGF-1 receptor in colon cancer cells switches on MEK, a survival signal, which may explain why IGF-1 receptor drugs worked poorly in patients. No official profile page was found.

highlights.WANG2026B: First author: showed in lung cancer cells and xenografts that Pdcd4 binds Rictor, breaks up mTORC2, lowers PFKFB3 and slows glycolysis and tumour growth.

sources: PubMed: Wang Q[Author] AND Yang HS[Author] AND Kentucky[Affiliation] (18 records)

Tang B.lab_name: Department of Urology, Institute of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Tang B.role: Urology researcher at West China Hospital and first author of a study explaining how kidney cancers escape mTOR inhibitor drugs, and how blocking NEK7 restores their effect
Tang B.sub: Department of Urology, Institute of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Everolimus and temsirolimus, two drugs that block mTOR, are used for advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common kidney cancer. Many tumours stop responding to them. In the Atlas study TAN2026 in Nature Communications, Bo Tang was first author of work that traces one escape route. The protein SPOP attaches a K63-linked chain of ubiquitin, a small tag protein, to ZMYND8. The tag keeps ZMYND8 out of phase-separated droplets, small membrane-less compartments inside the nucleus. Freed ZMYND8 pairs with ZHX2 to switch on the gene for NEK7, and NEK7 activates p70S6K, a growth kinase normally downstream of mTOR, by a route that mTOR drugs cannot block. A PROTAC, a molecule built to make the cell destroy a chosen protein, aimed at NEK7 restored sensitivity to everolimus. The evidence comes from cells and animal models, not from patients.

PubMed lists Tang at the Department of Urology and Institute of Urology of West China Hospital, Sichuan University in Chengdu. Because the name is very common, no other paper was tied to this person with enough confidence to include, and no official profile page was found.

highlights.TAN2026: First author: showed that SPOP-driven ubiquitination of ZMYND8 switches on NEK7 and lets kidney cancer cells activate p70S6K without mTOR, and that a NEK7 degrader restores everolimus sensitivity.

Tang B.note: A Bo Tang at the Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota) co-authored prostate-cancer protein-degradation papers with Haojie Huang in 2021-2023 (PMID 34158377, 36637424). If TAN2026's senior author Huang H is Haojie Huang, this is probably the same person's postdoc period; not confirmed, so not used.

Cao ZL.lab_name: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, Wenzhou Medical University (Taizhou, China)
Cao ZL.role: Urologist in Zhejiang who works with colleagues on inherited endocrine tumour syndromes and wrote a review re-examining how FLCN loss changes mTORC1 signalling in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
Cao ZL.sub: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University (2026) · Department of Urology / Oncologic and Urologic Surgery, 903rd PLA Hospital, Hangzhou Medical College (2023–2025)
story: Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is an inherited condition caused by faults in the FLCN gene. People with it can get benign skin bumps, air-filled cysts in the lungs that may cause a collapsed lung, and kidney tumours. For years the explanation was simple: lose FLCN and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on everywhere. In a 2026 review in Frontiers in Oncology (CAO2026), Zhi-Lie Cao, first author, with Wei-Ying Chen as senior author, argues that this picture does not fit the evidence. FLCN acts on the RagC/D switch proteins, which control only some mTORC1 targets, above all the MiT/TFE transcription factors. Losing both copies of FLCN lets these factors pile up in the nucleus and drives kidney tumours, while losing one copy may be enough for lung and skin changes. As a review, it reports no new experiments.

PubMed shows Cao as a urologist. In 2023 and 2025 papers the address is the urology and oncologic surgery department of the 903rd PLA Hospital of Hangzhou Medical College; by 2026 it is the Department of Urology of Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University. With Chen and Xiao-Ping Qi, Cao has co-authored case reports and literature reviews on rare tumours, including a primary seminoma of the prostate (2023) and families with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A caused by RET mutations (2025, 2026). No official profile page was found.

highlights.CAO2026: First author: argued in a review that FLCN controls mTORC1 selectively through RagC/D, and that FLCN gene dosage explains why kidney, lung and skin are affected differently.

Chen WY.lab_name: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, Wenzhou Medical University (Taizhou, China)
Chen WY.role: Urologist at Taizhou Hospital in Zhejiang and senior author of a review on why FLCN loss affects mTORC1 selectively in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
Chen WY.sub: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University, and Enze Hospital, Taizhou Enze Medical Center (papers 2023–2026)
story: In Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, faults in the FLCN gene cause skin bumps, lung cysts and kidney tumours. Wei-Ying Chen was the last author, usually the senior author, of the 2026 review CAO2026 in Frontiers in Oncology. The review argues against the old idea that FLCN loss simply turns on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, everywhere. FLCN works on the RagC/D switch proteins, which steer only some mTORC1 targets, especially the MiT/TFE transcription factors. Losing both FLCN copies lets these factors build up in the nucleus and drives kidney tumours, while one lost copy may be enough for lung and skin problems. It is a review of existing work, not a new experiment.

PubMed lists Chen in the Department of Urology of Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University, on papers from 2023 to 2026. Together with Zhi-Lie Cao and Xiao-Ping Qi, Chen has co-authored case reports and reviews on rare hereditary tumours, such as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A, a pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma syndrome now called multiple endocrine neoplasia type 5 (2024), and a primary seminoma of the prostate (2023). No official profile page was found.

highlights.CAO2026: Last author: supervised the review proposing that FLCN controls mTORC1 selectively through RagC/D and that gene dosage explains the different organ effects of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome.
